subject: english-literature
title: Freud, Oedipus and Critical Hamlets
welcome_lead: Survey the major critical readings of Hamlet — Bradleian character criticism, Freudian Oedipal, New Historicist, and feminist.
meta_desc: A-Level adventure on critical readings of Hamlet: Freud, Jones, Bradley, Greenblatt, and feminist Ophelias.
final_note: Every critical lens on Hamlet reveals what it cannot see — which is why the play has survived four centuries of theory.

concepts.def: Freud (1900) and Ernest Jones (1949) argue Hamlet's delay reflects unconscious identification with Claudius, who has acted out Hamlet's repressed desires.
A.C. Bradley's Shakespearean Tragedy (1904) treats Hamlet as a coherent psychological subject with a 'melancholy' temperament.
Stephen Greenblatt's Hamlet in Purgatory (2001) reads the play through Reformation theology and the suppression of Catholic purgatory.
Elaine Showalter's 'Representing Ophelia' (1985) recovers Ophelia from male critical projection, attending to her madness as social statement.
Readings rooted in stage history — Olivier (1948), Branagh (1996), Almereyda (2000) — show how each generation reinvents the play.
Theory that Q1 was reconstructed by an actor from memory; critics like Paul Werstine challenge this, complicating textual hierarchy.

walkthroughs.body_html: In a footnote to The Interpretation of Dreams (1900) Freud proposes that Hamlet cannot kill Claudius because Claudius has fulfilled Hamlet's own infantile wishes — to kill the father and possess the mother. Ernest Jones expanded this into Hamlet and Oedipus (1949). The reading's strength is its account of Hamlet's revulsion towards Gertrude in the closet scene; its weakness is its anachronism, projecting twentieth-century psychology onto an Early Modern play.

Greenblatt's Hamlet in Purgatory (2001) argues that the Ghost is theologically destabilising because Reformation England has officially abolished purgatory while popular belief retains it. The Ghost speaks like a Catholic soul ('confined to fast in fires'), but Protestant doctrine would identify him as demonic. Hamlet's hesitation is partly hermeneutic: how do you verify a spectre's confession?

Elaine Showalter's 'Representing Ophelia' (1985) catalogues the male critical tendency to read Ophelia as a decorative madwoman. Showalter recovers her songs as coded protest — they invoke sexual betrayal and patriarchal violence. Post-1985 productions (Lyndsey Turner, 2015; Robert Icke, 2017) treat her madness as politically legible, not merely pathological.
